texts.text: Weather Report

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: · Variable precipitation occurred over the past 7 days across agro-Manitoba. Once again, rains and isolated thunderstorms brought hail, strong winds, intense rain, and possible tornadoes swept through the majority of the province. The largest accumulations occurred in the Southwest near Boissevain and Souris, as well as the Northwest region in the already water-logged areas of San Clara, Ethelbert, Dauphin, Minnedosa, and Russell. Overland flooding and overflowing rivers and streams have caused many communities, including the City of Brandon, to declare local states of emergency. Weekly accumulations ranged from 9 (Sprague) to 188 mm (Boissevain). A tornado was confirmed in the Whyte Ridge neighborhood of Winnipeg on June 29.
texts.text: Variable precipitation occurred over the past 7 days across agro-Manitoba. Once again, rains and isolated thunderstorms brought hail, strong winds, intense rain, and possible tornadoes swept through the majority of the province. The largest accumulations occurred in the Southwest near Boissevain and Souris, as well as the Northwest region in the already water-logged areas of San Clara, Ethelbert, Dauphin, Minnedosa, and Russell. Overland flooding and overflowing rivers and streams have caused many communities, including the City of Brandon, to declare local states of emergency. Weekly accumulations ranged from 9 (Sprague) to 188 mm (Boissevain). A tornado was confirmed in the Whyte Ridge neighborhood of Winnipeg on June 29.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: · Climate normals for total accumulated precipitation from May 1 to July 5 range from 131 mm to 211 mm (Table 2) and are based on 30-year historical data. Since May 1, areas of the Northwest and Interlake regions have accumulated 220 mm of precipitation. Frequent precipitation events have brought seasonal accumulations well above normal for the entire Northwest and Interlake regions. Areas of the Central and Southwest region also have above-normal accumulations due to recent rainfall. Areas of the Northwest have accumulated more than 200% of normal precipitation. A few localized areas of the Central, and Eastern regions have seen accumulations under 80% of the 30-year average.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: · Excessive rainfall and saturated field conditions continue to delay forage harvest across much of Manitoba, with many producers waiting for extended periods of dry weather before resuming operations.
texts.text: Excessive rainfall and saturated field conditions continue to delay forage harvest across much of Manitoba, with many producers waiting for extended periods of dry weather before resuming operations.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: · Some producers took advantage of short weather windows to cut hay despite the risk of additional rainfall, as forage quality continues to decline with advancing maturity.
texts.text: Some producers took advantage of short weather windows to cut hay despite the risk of additional rainfall, as forage quality continues to decline with advancing maturity.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: · First-cut harvest is progressing across the province, with dairy operations in some areas already preparing for or beginning second-cut silage, while beef producers continue first-cut harvest.
texts.text: First-cut harvest is progressing across the province, with dairy operations in some areas already preparing for or beginning second-cut silage, while beef producers continue first-cut harvest.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: · Standing water and flooding have inundated hay land in several regions, delaying harvest, reducing forage quality, and in some cases preventing field access altogether.
texts.text: Standing water and flooding have inundated hay land in several regions, delaying harvest, reducing forage quality, and in some cases preventing field access altogether.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: · Hayfields in the Northwest Region, particularly around Dauphin, Ethelbert, and Ste. Rose, remain too wet for harvest and will require considerable drying before equipment can enter.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: · Most established alfalfa, grass hay stands, and pastures have generally tolerated the excess moisture with limited stand damage; however, localized flooding has caused significant losses in low-lying areas.
texts.text: Most established alfalfa, grass hay stands, and pastures have generally tolerated the excess moisture with limited stand damage; however, localized flooding has caused significant losses in low-lying areas.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: · Forage yields are expected to be adequate overall, but forage quality may be reduced due to delayed harvest and challenging drying conditions. Many producers are opting to produce silage rather than dry hay because of persistent wet weather.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: · Annual feed crop conditions remain variable across regions, with excess moisture negatively affecting growth in some areas. Some producers are considering seeding greenfeed on flooded acres if field conditions improve.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: · Corn continues to progress well in many areas, although localized hail damage, particularly in the Boissevain-Killarney area, has resulted in severe crop losses in some fields.

texts.label: list_item

texts.label: list_item

texts.text: Cases of foot rot are increasing in several regions due to prolonged wet conditions, and producers are encouraged to closely monitor cattle for signs of lameness and treat affected animals promptly.

texts.label: list_item

texts.orig: Southwest
texts.text: Southwest

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The Southwest region is experiencing very wet conditions following storms over the weekend. Most areas south of Highway #1 received 2-7 inches of rain, on top of the heavy rainfall from the previous week. Some crops are completely submerged, while others are partially under water.
texts.text: The Southwest region is experiencing very wet conditions following storms over the weekend. Most areas south of Highway #1 received 2-7 inches of rain, on top of the heavy rainfall from the previous week. Some crops are completely submerged, while others are partially under water.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Significant hail was reported near Cromer, Dand, Boissevain, Killarney, Wawanesa, and north of Hartney. Minor hail, approximately the size of a loonie, was reported near Reston and Brandon. Boissevain received golf ballsized hail, while Killarney experienced baseball-sized hail. Moderate lodging in cereal crops has also been observed in the Melita area.
texts.text: Significant hail was reported near Cromer, Dand, Boissevain, Killarney, Wawanesa, and north of Hartney. Minor hail, approximately the size of a loonie, was reported near Reston and Brandon. Boissevain received golf ballsized hail, while Killarney experienced baseball-sized hail. Moderate lodging in cereal crops has also been observed in the Melita area.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Overall, most of the Southwest region has good crop potential if conditions dry out soon. However, some flooded areas are unlikely to recover, and those crops will be lost. Despite these losses, conditions are not as severe as those reported in areas to the north and east.
texts.text: Overall, most of the Southwest region has good crop potential if conditions dry out soon. However, some flooded areas are unlikely to recover, and those crops will be lost. Despite these losses, conditions are not as severe as those reported in areas to the north and east.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Most pea fields have filled in and are just beginning to flower. They are approaching the stage for fungicide application if required; however, disease pressure remains low, and growers may be able to delay application. Winter wheat and fall rye are headed and continue to look good, with low disease levels reported so far. Producers were able to spray most of these acres before the major rainfall events began.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Spring-seeded cereals are at the flag leaf to early heading stage. Producers are attempting to apply fungicides, but many fields remain too wet, resulting in rutting during ground applications. Spray planes are heavily booked, which may affect the timing needed for optimal disease control. Leaf disease pressure remains relatively low at this time, but the current warm and humid conditions could increase disease development. Spring wheat crop condition is at 50% good and 50% average.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Most canola fields are at the full cabbage to early bolting stage, with the earliest fields approaching 30% flowering. Fungicide application timing is becoming critical for effective disease control. Higher cabbage seedpod weevil populations have been noted in the southern portion of the region, although there have been few reports of spraying. Weed control applications are still ongoing in some later-seeded canola fields.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Soybean crops have generally handled the wet conditions well, although some iron deficiency chlorosis (IDC) is beginning to appear. Most soybean fields are currently at the V3 to early flowering growth stage.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Corn and sunflower crops are progressing at an average pace. They continue to grow, and warmer temperatures would be beneficial for further development.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: Northwest
texts.text: Northwest

texts.label: text
texts.orig: An intense weather event moved in the Northwest Region to start the week. Rain began Monday and continued into Tuesday bringing significant amounts across the entire region. The large amounts across the region overwhelmed ditches/drains and rivers very quickly, causing significant overland flooding and damage to infrastructure. In addition to the entire Northwest region receiving damage, the Swan Valley area was affected for a second time. Water levels have since receded; however many fields are still affected by overland flooding and damage continues to be assessed.
texts.text: An intense weather event moved in the Northwest Region to start the week. Rain began Monday and continued into Tuesday bringing significant amounts across the entire region. The large amounts across the region overwhelmed ditches/drains and rivers very quickly, causing significant overland flooding and damage to infrastructure. In addition to the entire Northwest region receiving damage, the Swan Valley area was affected for a second time. Water levels have since receded; however many fields are still affected by overland flooding and damage continues to be assessed.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Manitoba Infrastructure damage was significant in this storm, with all previous repairs in the Swan Valley region washed away again. Much more additional damage was received across the entire region, making commuting impossible, as well as accessing fields.

texts.orig: Although some fields received timely herbicide applications, there are many fields that have missed the application window due to unfavourable conditions, including wet fields, rain and high winds.

texts.orig: Central
texts.text: Central

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The region continued to receive localized storms over the past week, with all areas receiving rain but volumes varying greatly. Producers have mostly wrapped up in-crop herbicide applications as more crops approach canopy closure. Only a very small proportion of farms are expected to make a second pass of herbicides. Producers are focusing on fungicide decisions, and insect monitoring. Many producers are relying on aerial applicators, especially due to the wet field conditions this year.

Soybeans are tolerating the wet conditions relatively well, although areas with prolonged saturation show reduced growth. texts.text: Eastern

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The Eastern region saw rainfall this last week ranging from 9.3 mm to 93.7 mm. Field conditions remain wet as showers continue to move through the region. Producers are hopeful for a few good drying days before fungicide applications in both wheat and canola get fully underway.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Herbicide applications are wrapping up with a few second pass applications on corn remaining. Wheat has moved into anthesis, and fungicide applications are planned this week. Canola is in full bloom, with fungicide applications also planned for this week.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Canola is at the bolting to 50% flower stage due to the long seeding window this spring. With the wet humid conditions, many producers are planning for a fungicide application to protect against sclerotinia; applications will begin this week.

texts.orig: Soybeans are at the first flower (R1) stage. Many fields have yellowed from the excess water, but most are out growing the stressed conditions. Sunflowers are delayed due to the wet conditions but are looking good for the most part.

texts.orig: Interlake
texts.text: Interlake

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Rainfall was significant this past week, with many areas experiencing saturation and flooding in low-lying spots. Many areas received substantial amounts of rain, along with some reports of hail. This consistent precipitation has led to saturated fields and flooding in low-lying areas across much of the South Interlake. The wet conditions are increasing the risk of root diseases in pulse crops and delaying herbicide applications. The cool and wet weather has also slowed crop development, complicating haying operations for farmers.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Manitoba Winter wheat and fall rye are beginning to flower, demonstrating strong stands. While conditions for winter cereal and fall rye remain generally good, areas affected by excess moisture are exhibiting signs of stress and hail damage.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Spring cereals are advancing into the tillering and stem elongation stages, with the first fields showing visible flag leaves. Most herbicide applications are complete, and producers are now concentrating on disease monitoring and fungicide operations. Spring wheat ranges from good to excellent in some areas, while others are rated as poor to fair. Spring cereal crops on drier ground are thriving, with about a quarter rated as excellent.

texts.orig: Corn is progressing well, reaching the V3 and V5 stages. Crop stands are excellent in some locations, while others impacted by excessive moisture are struggling. There are signs of uneven growth and nutrient stress in waterlogged fields.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Canola is making good progress, currently at the 5-leaf and bolting stages, with the earliest fields already flowering. Many producers are actively scouting for cabbage seedpod weevil using sweep nets, as they are being observed in large numbers feeding on buds, prompting anticipated insecticide applications. Oilseed crops in the flood affected southern regions are generally in poor condition, while those in northern areas have largely maintained normal development, although cool, wet weather has caused some delays.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Soybeans are currently in the 2 nd to 4 th trifoliolate stage, with the first round of herbicide applications mostly complete, leaving just a few second applications remaining. Some soybean fields are showing yellowing leaves due to excess moisture, while others are showing resilience. Peas are progressing well and are approaching canopy closure in most fields, currently at the 10-node stage. Among pulse crops, about 60% are in good condition, with the rest poor and showing signs of moisture stress.

texts.orig: Across the region, excessive moisture and persistent weed growth are the main concerns. Reports indicate moderate to severe damage from insects and strong winds. Flea beetles continue to be a problem, causing moderate damage, while minor issues from cutworms and cabbage seedpod weevils have also been noted.

texts.orig: Assessing Hail Damage in Cereal Crops
texts.text: Assessing Hail Damage in Cereal Crops

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Hail has affected crops in several areas of Manitoba over the last week. The amount of loss expected from a hail event depends on the severity of hail, crop type, and the growth stage of the crop. Assessments of damage should occur a few days after a hail event.
texts.text: Hail has affected crops in several areas of Manitoba over the last week. The amount of loss expected from a hail event depends on the severity of hail, crop type, and the growth stage of the crop. Assessments of damage should occur a few days after a hail event.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Wheat: Hail damage during jointing or in the boot stage is difficult to assess. Spikes can still pollinate and fill, and regrowth from new tillers can occur. The more advanced the wheat is at the time of hail the greater the yield loss. The greatest yield reduction from hail occurs in the milk stage.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Oats and Barley: Oats and barley will tiller and recover better from hail than wheat, especially prior to the boot stage. Grower experience has demonstrated that barley, hailed severely in the boot stage, has recovered to produce 70-80% of normal yield. Crop hailed prior to the boot stage should be left if stems or green tissue remains.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Corn: Leaf loss without damage to the growing point has a small impact on yield. Check corn for damage to the stem, and percent leaf defoliation. Between the V6 stage and tasseling percent yield loss is estimated to range from 0-34% depending on percent defoliation. For more information: How to assess corn after a hail event.
